extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetry and tragic drama, focusing on plot, character, diction, and other formal elements. Covers ancient poetics principles (mimesis), practical rules for dramatic construction, and criteria for critical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Imitation (Mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy, Comedy, dithyrambic poetry, and the music of the flute and lyre are modes of imitation; imitation is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand all poetic/arts activity as imitation; evaluate a work by how it imitates its objects. Different arts vary by medium, objects, and manner of imitation; aim to represent universal truths through faithful and artful imitation rather than mere reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium of imitation is rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (or melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and control the medium(s) appropriate to the effect: e.g., music + rhythm for lyric/dithyrambic effects; language (prose/verse) where verbal expression carries the imitation; combine media (rhythm, melody, language) deliberately when the form calls for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Imitation (Types of Characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action; these men must be either of a higher or a lower type (goodness and badness are distinguishing marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to depict characters as better, worse, or as they are. This distinction supports genre choices (tragedy vs comedy) and affects tone, moral portraiture, and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of Imitation (Form: Dramatic vs Narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric poetry), or pure drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the manner (dramatic presentation vs narrative) that best serves the imitation; be aware mixed forms exist. Ensure consistency of manner unless mixing is a deliberate artistic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Elements of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has six elements: Scenic Presentment (spectacle), Lyrical Song (chorus), Diction, Plot, Character, and Thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating tragedy, attend to each element and their interrelation; plot and internal elements (character, thought) are primary, but diction, song, and spectacle are important supporting elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (Mythos) — primacy and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, or the representation of the action, is of primary importance; the Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot as a self-contained whole with a clear beginning, middle, and end and sufficient scale to produce the intended effect. Prioritize causal and structural integrity over incidental episodes or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose and is the second-most important element after plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose actions flow from consistent moral purpose; use probability/necessity to make character behavior convincing. Characters should be appropriate to plot needs and believable as moral agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought, or the intellectual element, may be expressed either by dramatic speeches (composed according to rhetoric) or through the dramatic incidents which speak for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to articulate themes, arguments, and intelligible motivations; ensure speeches and incidents express thought in ways appropriate to dramatic action and intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction, or language in general, concerns the words and modes of speech admissible in poetry; it largely falls within the domain of the art of declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words, figures (especially metaphor), and modes of speech that suit the genre and characters. Balance elevation with clarity; diction should serve thought and plot, not obscure them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song / Choral Odes (Melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical Song (choral odes) is one of the external elements of Tragedy and should be an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choral odes so they advance or illuminate the action; avoid choral passages that are merely decorative or interruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic Presentment (Spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenic Presentment (spectacle) is an external element of Tragedy—an accessory that can be vivid but should not be relied upon to produce the tragic emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend on spectacle to generate pity and fear; the emotional effect should arise primarily from plot and character, not scenery or stagecraft. Spectacle may enhance but must not substitute for structural or ethical depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Unity (Unity of Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists not in unity of hero, but in unity of Action: the parts must be organically connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all incidents serve the single action. Avoid extraneous subplots that undermine the organic unity; a good plot has one main action with coherently related parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal Sequence (Probable or Necessary Sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic Unity can be attained only by the observance of poetic as distinct from historic truth; the rule of probable or necessary sequence is applied to the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so each follows reasonably (by probability or necessity) from what precedes. Poetic truth (the universal) allows compression and selection, but events should cohere causally for audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be of adequate magnitude: large enough to be complete but not so extensive as to dilute effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope that permits development of the action to its proper emotional and thematic resolution; avoid both over-long diffusion (weakening effect) and excessive compression (truncation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots involve change without reversal or recognition; Complex plots include reversal (peripeteia), recognition (anagnorisis), and tragic incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to employ complex structures (which can produce stronger catharsis via recognition and reversal) or simpler ones. Use reversals and recognitions only when organically motivated by the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden Reversal or Recoil of the Action (peripeteia) is a change from one state to its opposite, contributing to the tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct reversals as natural consequences of prior actions; avoid arbitrary or unmotivated reversals designed merely for surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is the discovery by which a person’s true identity or situation is revealed (various kinds exist), and it plays a key role in tragic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition to transform the audience's understanding in ways that are plausibly rooted in the plot; effective recognitions often pair with reversal to heighten pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident / Suffering (Pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic or disastrous incident (pathos) is a component of complex plots that produces suffering and contributes to catharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure suffering arises from the action and character, not from spectacle; design incidents so pity and fear flow logically from what has gone before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for the Tragic Hero (Change of Fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune and the character of the hero are requisite to an ideal Tragedy; the unhappy ending is more truly tragic than poetic justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray a protagonist of noble or better-than-average character whose downfall results from error or frailty (hamartia) plausibly linked to moral purpose; avoid purely villainous or purely blameless figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting Pity and Fear (Catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself; to produce them by Scenery or Spectacular effect is against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plot and character to make emotional responses inevitable; resist cheap visual or sensational tricks that manufacture emotion without moral or causal grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Compositional Rule — Embodiment and Enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play or enact scenes as a drafting technique to deepen psychological realism and ensure actions feel internally motivated and performable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Compositional Rule — Outline Before Episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a structural skeleton (plot outline/unity of action) to avoid digression; then expand episodes so each serves the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with Complication and Denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the Complication (débours) and Dénouement (resolution) of the Plot; especially the Dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft complications that lead inevitably to a denouement with satisfying causal logic; avoid forced or patchwork resolutions (including deus ex machina).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Choral Odes Organic and Avoid Epic Overload
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole; not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each lyric or choral passage advances theme/action or deepens character; avoid long epic-style digressions or excessive background material that weakens dramatic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Diction and Figures (Metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry: including Metaphor in particular. Poetry should combine elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors and elevated diction to enhance meaning, but keep clarity in view. Metaphor should illuminate character/thought; obscure or forced figurative language is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Truth vs Historical Particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an expression of the Universal; History is of the Particular. Poetic truth (what ought to be or what is generally true) governs poetic construction over literal historical fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary, alter or compress events to reveal universal human truths; prioritize plausibility of motive and consequence over strict factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility: Probable Impossibility over Improbable Possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The impossible must be justified by artistic requirements or by received opinion; with respect to art, a probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including seemingly impossible elements, justify them by artistic purpose or convention so they feel 'probable' within the work’s terms; avoid unlikely but unsupported incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of Criticism — Five Objection Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections arise because things are censured as impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or evaluating a work, address objections under these five heads and answer by reference to the twelve explanatory heads (plot, character, diction, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Considerations (Cultivated vs Popular)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the more refined art is the higher, then Epic is addressed to a cultivated audience; Tragedy is sometimes thought to address a less refined public and to use gesture to compensate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust complexity, diction, and reliance on spectacle with regard to intended audience; but do not excuse structural weaknesses by blaming audience taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive Tools for Difficult Passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties of interpretation may be resolved by due regard to diction: metaphor, accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of construction, or the usage of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting obscure lines, consider multiple linguistic devices (metaphor, syntax, accentuation, punctuation conventions) and plausible alternative readings before judging them faulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Criterion: Tragedy vs Epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has concentrated effect, vividness in reading and representation, and greater unity; these properties often make Tragedy the higher art compared to Epic, which is longer and less unified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare modes by their capacity to attain their specific ends: choose form and scale appropriate to the desired concentrated emotional and intellectual effect.
